newsitem.title: IRAN: New jolt hits Iran, victims of first quake await aid.
newsitem.headline: New jolt hits Iran, victims of first quake await aid.

text.p: Another earthquake hit Iran on Monday, two days after a massive quake devastated the country's eastern region killing nearly 2,400 people.

The new quake, registering 4.8 on the Richter scale, hit the cities of Ardabil and Nir in northwestern Iran, but there was no report yet on possible loss of life or damage to property, the official news agency IRNA reported.

It struck as survivors of Saturday's force 7.1 quake in eastern Iran were still scrambling among the ruins of their homes and burying their dead as they waited for international aid in response to a government appeal.
In the rubble of the poor villages hit hardest by the quake, men, women and children wept and wailed as they picked through the debris of their mud-brick homes searching for something to salvage.
But nothing seemed to be undamaged, and only the trees were left standing. The survivors were left with nothing but their own lives.

Women wailed and beat their faces violently in grief. A man mourned over the broken, bloody body of a child, and middle-aged men comforted each other as they stood sobbing among the ruins of their devastated homes.
Many tremors with magnitude of more than four have hit Ardabil since February 28 when an earthquake with an intensity of 5.5 jolted the region, killing about 1,000 people and injuring at least 2,600.
The United Nations and Iranian officials said the death toll -- nearly 2,400 people -- from Saturday's earthquake was unlikely to change drastically as the rescue operation was nearly done.

"Our team called from the area this morning. The impression is that the death toll announced yesterday will not change drastically because the rescue work in Birjand is completed and in Qaen it is 85 to 90 percent finished," said Andres Frismark, deputy resident representative in Iran of the U.N. Development Programme.
"So we don't expect any surprises in terms of the death toll beyond what we heard. There is still rescue work in a few villages so the number might rise slightly."

Iran's Interior Minister Ali Mohammad Besharati said on Sunday rescue teams had completed operations in Birjand and hoped to finish soon in Qaen. Authorities expected to reach definitive casualty figures after the rescue operations, which they hoped would be concluded on Sunday night, he added.
Human resources in terms of rescue and relief were good, Frismark told Reuters by telephone from Tehran.
"They are doing extremely well, a marvellous job. But what has become critical now is the stocks.
"The Red Crescent, which has warehouses in most disaster-prone areas, has stockpiles which are reaching a weak level and need to be replenished. That has become critical.
"Help and assistance is not just needed for that purpose but also for now. Immediate help is needed urgently," he said.

Quake-prone Iran, accustomed to dealing with natural disasters, on Sunday appealed through the United Nations for international aid to help relieve the suffering of survivors in 200 devastated villages.
Iran's Arab neighbours, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates said they were flying in aid. So did Egypt.
The United States and France said they were ready to help.
Some 6,000 people were injured in the quake.
Frismark said 10,000 families, making up to 50,000 people, have been displaced by the quake. Some had not lost their homes, but were living outdoors waiting for aftershocks to stop.
Iran said 150 aftershcoks have been registered in the area.
Initial estimates put the extent of damages in the region at 230 billion rials ($77 million).

Some 4,300 relief workers have set up 9,000 tents and Iran has asked for food, medicine, tents, clothing, water tanks, clothing and four-wheel drive vehicles to use in relief works in the mountainous area near the Afghan border.
